title: India's Supreme Court Signs Landmark MOU with Russia on AI in Courts, Drawing Constitutional Scrutiny
excerpt: CJI Surya Kant's Moscow agreement promises tech collaboration and judicial exchanges, but legal scholars question whether the court overstepped its constitutional role
body:
The Supreme Courts of India and Russia signed a first-of-its-kind Memorandum of Understanding in Moscow on June 24, marking a formal commitment to share judicial technology, training programmes, and best practices between two legal systems that evolved through starkly different traditions. The agreement was signed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Chairman of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation Igor Krasnov, during a visit that also took CJI Kant to the 14th St Petersburg International Legal Forum.

The MOU covers three broad areas: exchange of experiences in using technology for court administration, professional training and capacity-building for judges and court staff, and the establishment of a Joint Working Group to develop strategies for sustained institutional engagement between the two judiciaries.

## AI as a Tool, Not a Judge

At the centre of the agreement is a shared interest in artificial intelligence and its role in the administration of justice. Speaking at the Russian Supreme Court, CJI Surya Kant drew a careful line between AI as a judicial aid and AI as a decision-maker.

"Artificial Intelligence may assist Judges by organising information, facilitating translations, generating transcripts, and streamlining administrative processes," he said. "It cannot determine outcomes, assess witness credibility, evaluate evidence, or exercise judicial discretion."

The remarks reflected India's evolving approach to AI in its courts. The Supreme Court recently notified Draft Regulations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Judiciary, which seek to ensure that AI tools are deployed responsibly while preserving judicial independence and human oversight. India has already built and deployed tools such as SUVAS (Supreme Court Vidhik Anuvaad Software), which translates judgments from English into 16 regional languages, and Su Sahay, an AI-powered chatbot that helps litigants, lawyers, and the public navigate court procedures and case status.

CJI Kant also highlighted India's broader digital transformation in the judiciary — digitisation of court records, virtual hearings, video conferencing, and online access to case information — as models that could inform the Joint Working Group's agenda.

## Global South Solidarity and Unequal Scrutiny

The Moscow visit was not limited to the bilateral MOU. At the St Petersburg International Legal Forum, CJI Kant delivered an address titled "Equal Justice, Equal Law: Access as the Measure of International Law's Humanity," in which he argued that countries in the Global East and Global South face disproportionate international scrutiny despite continuing to grapple with the long-term consequences of colonial rule, institutional challenges, and socio-economic inequality.


![Memorandum of Understanding — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/26/GCC_and_Switzerland_HoS_Davos_2026.jpg)


"Powerful and economically advanced countries are not always subjected to the same level of scrutiny despite having their own shortcomings in compliance with international obligations," he observed, pointing to the complexity of challenges faced by developing nations — challenges that the original framers of international legal instruments may not have fully anticipated.

The comments positioned India alongside other developing nations pushing for a more equitable international legal order, a stance that resonates with India's broader foreign policy posture under Prime Minister Modi.

## A Constitutional Propriety Debate

Not everyone welcomed the MOU. Legal scholar Sanjay Kumar Singh published a detailed analysis questioning whether the Supreme Court, as an institution, has the constitutional authority to execute memoranda of understanding with foreign judicial bodies.

Singh's argument centres on the constitutional division of powers: the conduct of foreign affairs — including the negotiation and execution of international agreements — falls squarely within the domain of the Union Executive under India's constitutional framework, not the judiciary. The MOU, he notes, is explicitly between the Supreme Court of India and the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, not between India and Russia as states.

"There exists no higher forum to correct the Court when it errs in the conduct of its own affairs; the discipline must therefore be self-imposed," Singh wrote. He argued that whatever the court does in its institutional capacity "carries an exemplary force" that instructs every other organ of the state, making it essential that the court be "the most scrupulous as to the vires and the propriety of its own acts."

The critique raises a serious institutional question: even if the substance of the MOU — technology sharing, judicial training, exchange visits — is unobjectionable, does the form of the agreement cross a line that the Constitution draws between the judiciary and the executive?

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs with pending legal matters in India — property disputes, family law cases, commercial litigation — the MOU's focus on digital infrastructure and AI-assisted translation carries practical significance. Improved access to court information, multilingual case documents, and virtual hearing capabilities could reduce the friction of navigating India's judicial system from abroad.

More broadly, the constitutional debate around the MOU reflects the kind of institutional evolution that diaspora legal professionals and scholars follow closely. India's judiciary has been increasingly assertive in its institutional engagements, and the Moscow agreement is likely to fuel ongoing conversations about the appropriate boundaries of judicial autonomy in a parliamentary democracy.

The MOU itself is a framework document — its impact will depend on whether the Joint Working Group produces concrete deliverables or remains a statement of intent. But as a signal of India's willingness to internationalise its judicial modernisation agenda, the Moscow agreement is significant, even as the constitutional questions it raises remain unresolved.
